concept.name: Broken-wing butterfly
concept.definition: A broken-wing butterfly is a butterfly variant in which the distances between the middle strike and the two wing strikes are unequal — typically the far wing is placed further away (or a strike is skipped), skewing the payoff so that risk is reduced or eliminated on one side at the cost of added exposure on the other.
concept.intuition: It is a butterfly bent out of symmetry: you give up the balanced payoff to create a trade that can profit, or at least not lose, on the side you fear less.
concept.mechanics: Construction remains 1 long - 2 short - 1 long in the same option type and expiration, but the wing widths differ (e.g., $5 on one side, $10 on the other). The asymmetric strikes shift the peak and can turn the position into a net-credit trade with no loss on one side and an embedded vertical-spread loss on the other.
concept.formula: Value at expiration (call version, strikes K1 < K2 < K3, K2 - K1 != K3 - K2) = max(S_T - K1, 0) - 2 x max(S_T - K2, 0) + max(S_T - K3, 0) - net premium.
concept.failure_modes: The 'no risk on one side' property depends on entering for at least zero cost and breaks down after fees and slippage; the widened wing side carries a larger maximum loss than a symmetric butterfly, which traders underestimating the asymmetry can miss.
concept.misconceptions: It is not a defect-free butterfly — the broken wing trades one risk profile for another; calling it a 'free' directional bet ignores the embedded debit/credit spread exposure on the wide side.
concept.example: Buy the $95 call, sell two $100 calls, buy the $110 call (broken 5/10 wings) for a $0.20 credit. If XYZ finishes at or below $95, keep the $20 credit; the peak value is $5.20 at $100, and beyond $110 the embedded $5-wide spread loses.
